subtype: Approach: silent endurance hoping it stops [Pitfall]
passage:
Madhuri: hey. you've missed school 3 days this week
Ritu: just tired
Madhuri: last week too. and you stopped coming to lunch
Ritu: I'm fine
Madhuri: I don't think you are. is it the back row group?
Ritu: it's been going on since July. I thought if I ignored it, it would stop
Madhuri: and it hasn't?
Ritu: no. now I keep thinking about not going in at all. it feels like the only way to get a break
Madhuri: that sounds really heavy. I'm glad you told me. it isn't your fault
Madhuri: tell your mum tonight. tomorrow I'll come with you to see the counsellor and stay next to you
Ritu: ok. mum tonight. I'll try
Ritu: told her. she stopped everything and just listened
Ritu: she said none of it is my fault and she's emailing the counsellor now so we can go in tomorrow morning
Madhuri: I'm really glad. I'll meet you at the gate

qa.q: Since when had it been going on, according to Ritu?
qa.a: It had been going on since July.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when saying 'I thought if I ignored it, it would stop'?
qa.a: Ritu felt hopeful at first and is now worn down and stuck, since ignoring it has not worked and staying away seems like the only relief.

qa.q: What could Ritu and Madhuri do to make sure it is handled safely, and why?
qa.a: Ritu could go to the counsellor the next morning with Ritu's mum and Madhuri, and keep them updated, because adults can act on it and Ritu no longer carries it alone.

qa.q: What is it like for Madhuri to hear this?
qa.a: Madhuri is probably worried and caring, noticing the missed days and the missed lunches, and glad Ritu opened up. 🤍

grounding: The student ignores the bullying and says nothing for months, and it continues, self-confidence drops, and avoiding school starts to seem like the only relief.
